tags.gist: Says evaluation should rest on team performance whenever an accountable clinician sees the output, which requires fixing the output's workflow position.
Cites an autonomous retinopathy screener whose labeling asks physicians to review results they have no means to check against missed cases.
Cites a vignette experiment in which patient trust fell when a clinician saw AI output concurrently and rose when the clinician assessed first.
Recommends treating the output's workflow position as a property of the device being evaluated, specified in the intended use as precisely as the output.
Answers that team performance applies when an accountable clinician sees the output, and that the paper's phrase about actual use leaves one thing unspecified.
Analyzes the retinopathy screener's authorization: the physician review step in labeling cannot catch cases the autonomous classification missed.
Reports preregistered experiments where only the order of clinician assessment and AI support changed, and patient trust changed significantly with it.
Asks CDRH to fix display timing, prior independent assessment and accountability in the intended use, and to ask which ordering was tested and enforced.
